ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism-m.set_intro: A solid nonconducting sphere of radius $10\text{ cm}$ carries a charge spread uniformly through its volume. The graph shows the magnitude of the electric field as a function of the distance $r$ from the center. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$.

stimulus.description: Electric field magnitude versus distance from the center

items.stem: What is the total charge on the sphere?

options.why: Uses $E_sR/k$, forgetting that the distance enters squared.
At $r=R$ the field is the peak value $E_s=kQ/R^2$, so $Q=E_sR^2/k=4.00\text{ nC}$.
Omits the factor $4\pi$, $\varepsilon_0E_sR^2$.
Reads the field at $r=2R$ instead of at the surface, then uses $E R^2/k$ with $R$.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism
blueprint.concept: Two questions about the field graph of a uniformly charged sphere
student_thinking: Read the peak field at the surface
Use the exterior inverse-square field for the potential difference

key_conditions.condition: the charge is uniformly distributed through the volume
key_conditions.evidence: the shared description states a uniform volume charge

must_include: peak at the radius of the sphere

misconceptions.description: Uses $E_sR/k$, forgetting that the distance enters squared.
Omits the factor $4\pi$, $\varepsilon_0E_sR^2$.
Reads the field at $r=2R$ instead of at the surface, then uses $E R^2/k$ with $R$.

verification.independent_path: the charge and the potential difference are recomputed from the closed forms of the field and a numerical integration

items.stem: What is the potential difference between the surface ($r=R$) and the point $r=3R$? ($V_R-V_{3R}$)

options.why: Uses the potential at the surface, $kQ/R=E_sR$.
Uses the uniform-field estimate with the peak field, $E_s\,(2R)$.
Evaluates $kQ(1/R-1/(9R))$, squaring the radius ratio.
Outside the sphere $E=kQ/r^2$, so $\Delta V=kQ(1/R-1/(3R))=\tfrac23E_sR=240\text{ V}$.

stimulus.description: Charging current measured at several times

items.stem: What is the emf of the battery?

options.why: Uses the current at $t=\tau$ in $IR$.
Doubles the product, $2I_0R$.
Uses the final current times $R$ at $3\tau$.
At $t=0$ the capacitor acts as a wire, so $\varepsilon=I_0R=15.0\text{ V}$.

blueprint.concept: Two questions about the charging current of an RC circuit

Find the time at which the current has fallen to $1/e$

key_conditions.condition: the capacitor was uncharged at $t=0$ and the battery is ideal
key_conditions.evidence: the shared description states an uncharged capacitor and an ideal battery

misconceptions.description: Uses the current at $t=\tau$ in $IR$.
Doubles the product, $2I_0R$.
Uses the final current times $R$ at $3\tau$.

verification.independent_path: the table values are recomputed from the circuit equation with an RK4 integration

items.stem: What is the capacitance of the capacitor?

Reads $\tau$ as the time at which the current is half of $I_0$ and uses $\tau/R$.
Uses $3\tau/R$, reading the last row as $\tau$.
The current falls to $I_0/e$ at $t=\tau$, so $\tau=40\text{ ms}$ and $C=\tau/R=8.00\,\mu\text{F}$.

ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism-m.set_intro: A long straight cylindrical wire of radius $2\text{ mm}$ carries a current distributed uniformly over its cross-section. The graph shows the magnitude of the magnetic field as a function of the distance $r$ from the axis, inside and outside the wire. Use $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$.

stimulus.description: Magnetic field magnitude versus distance from the axis

items.stem: What is the total current in the wire?

options.why: Uses $4\pi$ in place of $2\pi$.
Outside the wire $B=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)$; at $r=R$, $I=2\pi RB_s/\mu_0=10.0\text{ A}$.
Reads the field at $r=R/2$, half the peak, instead of at the surface.
Leaves out the factor $2\pi$, $B_sR/\mu_0$.

blueprint.concept: Two questions about the field graph of a long wire with uniform current density
student_thinking: Read the peak field at the wire's surface
Use Ampère's law with the enclosed area

key_conditions.condition: the current is uniform over the cross-section

Reads the field at $r=R/2$, half the peak, instead of at the surface.

verification.independent_path: the total and enclosed currents are recomputed from the Ampère law for each radius

items.stem: What current is enclosed by a circle of radius $R/2$ centered on the axis?

options.why: Takes the current enclosed to be an eighth of the total, using the cube of the ratio.
Takes the current enclosed to be half of the total, since the radius is half.
Takes the current enclosed to be the whole current.
The current density is uniform, so the enclosed current scales as the area: $I(R/2)^2/R^2=2.50\text{ A}$.
